title.en: Enki and Ninhursag: The Paradise of Dilmun and the Eight Healing Goddesses
title.zh: 恩基與寧胡爾薩格：迪爾蒙樂園與八位癒合女神

region.en: Nippur, Iraq (tablet findspot; Dilmun traditionally identified with Bahrain)
region.zh: 伊拉克尼普爾（泥板出土地；迪爾蒙傳統上比定為巴林）

texts.period: Old Babylonian copies (c. 1750-1600 BCE) of earlier Sumerian poems; principal tablets: Nippur finds (e.g. Ni-series), University of Pennsylvania Museum

summary.en: In the pure land of Dilmun, where nothing is sick and no crow caws, Enki waters the earth; the mother-goddess Ninhursag bears him a line of goddesses, and when Enki eats eight plants she has grown, eight of his organs sicken — until the fox wins her return, and she gives birth to eight healing deities, among them Ninti, Lady of the Rib.
summary.zh: 純淨之邦迪爾蒙，無病無疾、無鴉啼無獅噬；恩基灌水其地；母神寧胡爾薩格為之生女神一系；恩基竊食其八草，八臟俱病；狐智請回母神，母神遂生八位癒合之神，其中有寧提——『肋骨之女』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary text of a dead tradition.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of ETCSL 1.1.1, lines 1-30: The land Dilmun is pure, the land Dilmun is clean... In Dilmun the raven utters no cry, the lion kills not, the wolf snatches not the lamb... its sicknesses are not — for Enki has blessed it: 'may the city drink healthful waters'. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of ETCSL 1.1.1, lines 1-30; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of ETCSL 1.1.1 (ending): Eight plants have sprung up; Enki eats them one by one in the marsh; Ninhursag curses him: 'until thou art dead, I shall not look upon thee with life-giving eye'; eight of his organs fail — until the fox offers to bring her back; she returns, seats him by her vulva, and for each ailing part bears a deity: 'for my rib — Ninti, the Lady of the rib.' Not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The Sumerian paradise narrative — Eden's oldest Near Eastern relative — combines a creation-blessing, a genealogy of goddesses born from desire, and a sickness-and-healing plot whose rib pun was noted by every generation of Genesis scholars.

DILMUN: THE PURE LAND. Dilmun, a land traditionally identified with Bahrain or the eastern shore, is blessed before it is real: 'In Dilmun the raven utters no cry... the lion kills not... no one says: my eyes are sick... no one says: my head is sick.' But it lacks one thing — fresh water. Ninhursag, the mother-goddess ('Lady of the Mountain'), asks Enki, lord of the waters, for the gift; he answers: 'May the city of Dilmun drink healthful waters' — and Enki, god of the sweet water (abzu), brings the Tigris and Euphrates to her: he mates with her in the marsh, and his seed pours into her womb. She bears nine days, and Ninsar ('Lady Green Herb', the plant-goddess) is born.

THE CHAIN OF BIRTHS. The narrative repeats: Ninsar grows lush in the reed-beds; Enki desires her and lies with her; she bears Ninkurra ('Lady of the Pasture'); Enki lies with her; she bears Uttu, 'the Lady of Plants' — the spider-weaver of the vegetable world. Ninhursag, angered, warns Uttu and removes Enki's seed from her; Uttu asks for fruit, and Enki, with the gardener's help, fills her with apples, cucumbers, and grapes — the seed falls into the earth, and from it eight plants sprout in the marsh.

THE EATING AND THE SICKNESS. Enki, walking the marsh with his vizier Isimud, sees the eight plants and eats them, one by one — his steward warns each time, 'My lord, the plant!' — he eats. Ninhursag, furious ('was he to eat them all?'), curses him: she will not look on him with the life-giving eye until he is dead, and she vanishes. Eight of Enki's organs sicken one by one — jaw, tooth, mouth, hand, rib, foot, side, head — and the great gods sit helpless: 'the fox said to Enlil: shall I bring her? I know her place' — the fox, for a reward, fetches Ninhursag from the mountain; she returns, seats Enki by her vulva, and asks each part: 'my jaw aches... my tooth aches... my rib aches' — and for each she bears a deity to heal it: Abu for the plants? (Abu, Nintul, Ninsutu, Ninkasi — Lady Beer — Dazimua, Ninki, Nanshe? and Ningiri? — the canonical list includes Ninti, 'Lady of the Rib' or 'Lady of the Leaf' (ti = both), the pun that later readers compared to Eve, 'mother of all living', built from a rib).

END: THE BLESSING OF SUMER. Healed, Enki blesses his recovered organs and assigns them cults — Urim, Nippur, Eridu, Meluhha — and the poem ends with the goddess's praise: Ninhursag, 'who has given birth to all the gods', is exalted. The paradise episode of Dilmun (pure, watered, painless) becomes the scriptural prototype of the garden-of-god narratives of the Near East.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds the theology of water (Enki's blessing makes paradise), the horticultural economy (goddesses as plants; healing as childbirth), and the medical ideology of healing deities born from sickness; its rib-leaf pun entered the comparative literature of Genesis; and its Dilmun frames the Persian Gulf as a trade paradise in Sumerian economy.
narrative.zh: 迪爾蒙為純淨之邦：鴉不啼、獅不噬、無病無疾，惟缺淡水。寧胡爾薩格請恩基灌水，恩基許之，於沼地交合，九日生寧薩爾（綠草女神）；恩基復與寧薩爾合，生寧庫拉；再生烏圖（植物女神）。寧胡爾薩格怒而告烏圖避之；烏圖求果，恩基以蘋果、黃瓜、葡萄誘之；種子落地，沼中生八草。恩基與侍臣伊西姆得行沼上，侍臣每草皆勸『主，草也！』而恩基一一食之。寧胡爾薩格大怒詛之：『不與汝生命之眼，至死方休』，遂隱。恩基八臟次第病——頜、齒、口、手、肋、足、脅、首——眾神束手。狐言『能請其歸』，受賞請回母神；母神歸，使恩基坐己陰之前，逐一問病，逐病生一神以癒之：頜生阿布、齒生寧圖勒、口生寧蘇圖、手生寧卡西（啤酒女神）、肋生寧提（『肋骨之女』；ti 兼『肋』『葉』之音，與夏娃『眾生之母』之雙關為比較文學經典）、足生達茲木阿、脅生寧基、首生寧吉利。癒後恩基賜福諸器而封其祀——烏爾、尼普爾、埃利都、梅魯哈。母神『生眾神者』受頌。功能：水之創世論、園藝經濟之女神系、病而愈之醫學神學、以及近東樂園敘事之原型。

functions: Prototype of Near Eastern paradise narratives (pure land, watered, painless)
Theology of water: Enki's blessing as the making of paradise
Medical ideology: healing deities born from diseased organs
Gulf economy: Dilmun as the trade-paradise of Sumerian commerce

variants.name: Genesis 2-4 parallel
variants.summary: Shares the garden, the curse-on-eating, the sickness of the body, and — famously — the rib woman ('Ninti'/'Eve, mother of all living'); the pun (Sumerian ti = 'rib' and 'leaf') is the classic comparandum.

variants.name: Enki and the World Order (ETCSL 1.1.3)
variants.summary: A companion poem in which Enki, healed and enthroned, assigns offices to every deity and land — the administrative sequel to the paradise narrative.

variants.name: Dilmun in later Mesopotamian and Gulf texts
variants.text_tradition: Administrative and epic references (Gilgamesh XI's Dilmun; Persian Gulf trade archives)
variants.summary: Dilmun survives as the pure land of Utnapishtim's dwelling and as the copper-and-pearl entrepot of Gulf trade — myth and economy kept the name alive for two millennia.
